Long Haul Covid [5829]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
COVID-19 symptoms usually bring to mind flu-like symptoms, plus trouble breathing or losing your sense of taste. Many people can even get by with minimal impact on their lives even with an active infection. Some won’t have any symptoms at all.

COVID-19 symptoms can be scary enough in the moment, but now we are beginning to see the long-term effects the virus has on some people.
‘Long haul:’ Coronavirus survivors battling unexpected symptoms for months
Studies estimate one in 10 COVID-19 survivors will become ‘long haulers’.

Author Helen Moffat rates a good day as being able to stay awake the whole day. She contracted covid earlier this year but her symptoms have lingered. Most people speak about enervating lethargy, reduced lung capacity, arythmia, brain fog, chest pain, arthritis to name but a few.
Helen struggles a lot with her memory and says for someone who is used to crafting words, she, at times, can spend ages on just one sentence.

And some days are better than others but she feels a long way from the person she was before.

The medical fraternity is only now starting to look at the complications post disease. The scientific research has largely been focussed on finding a vaccine. But hospitals are concerned about patients who are suffering from consequences, months after their first infection.

Dr Karen van der Plas, in Cape Town, has now devoted her practise to helping people. She says that we are at the early stages of understanding the virus and its complications. And very little is known about the premanent damage that Covid may have on the organs.

Dr Salim Abdool Karim says that research conducted overses that 30% of COVID-19 patients had not returned to normal health conditions two or three weeks after testing.

However, it’s still pretty mysterious as to who will have these impacts and why. Scientists think that weak antibody responses or inflammatory reactions as possible reasons for the virus to stick around a long time, but there’s no perfect formula for knowing how your body will react to the virus.

One of the more serious possible long-term repercussions of COVID-19 is heart damage. A study released in July of 100 COVID-19 patients showed that in most of those who had supposedly recovered two months prior were still showing cardiac problems, ranging from structural changes to biomarkers that indicate cardiac injury.

Dr van der Plas says that that 78% of ‘recovered’ patients had evidence of ongoing heart involvement means that the heart is involved in a majority of patients, even if Covid-19 illness does not scream out with the classical heart symptoms, such as anginal chest pain.

Haji Mohammed Dawjee contracted covid about 5 months ago and has written quite prolifically of how it has impacted her life. She has a new baby and just feels that she does not have the energy that she would like to have to look after him. She is also a journalist and well spoken.

COVID-19 is a respiratory virus, so perhaps it’s not shocking that some of the long-term issues would be in the respiratory system. One study from August shows that some long term recoveries from COVID-19 infections may include from chronic cough, fibrotic lung disease, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary vascular disease.

I am trying to get an interview with a nurse who has long term covid.

The road to recovery seems long, Dr van der Plas, is helping her patients gradually build up their strength through gentle exercise and good nutrition. She believes that in years to come doctors will ask their patients whether they had covid or not to understand the pathology of the patient.

What burden will this place on an already over strained medical maternity. We also need to look at this should South Africa be poised at the brink of a second wave of the virus.

Long Haul Script

Phoeda
“Honestly it might sound dramatic but it feels like I have been hit by a train on the worst days and I can’t get out of bed, I really can’t do much. I only get up to eat that’s all I can do.”

V/O
And it’s a journey for her that has no end in sight for now. 23 year old Dr Pheidah Ngoepe contracted COVID-19 over 7 months ago and this disease has left her debilitated.
Author and activist Helen Moffat, contracted the virus in March 2020 and
says that everyday is an immense struggle.

Helen
“This illness is taking the form of an advent calendar, every day a new window opens and a new symptom pops out. Then the gastro started and the stomach cramps and the nausea and then I went out on night to look at the stars and planet and why are there two of mars and the blurred vision had started.”

Link
It’s not unusual for viruses to cause after effects…

What doctors are now seeing though is for long haul patients recovering from the disease is not the end of their ordeal, it’s just the beginning.


V/O
It has been described as the Covid that won’t go away.
Both Helen and Pheidah have been diagnosed with what is now called Post Covid Syndrome or Long Haul Covid, which loosely means people who have experienced COVID symptoms for longer that 28 days.
Coronavirus "long-haulers" continue to experinece symptoms like fevers, extreme exhaustion, brain fog, memory loss, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, and in Helen’s case blurry vision. She no longer feels that it is safe to drive her car.






Prof
“When we first heard about this disease, we had no idea what it's presenting features were, what shape or form it would take, but we have been learning almost on a daily basis.”

V/O
Professor Salim Abdool Karim, is South Africa’s Anthony Fauci and the co-Chair of Ministerial Advisory Committee on Covid-19

Prof
“If I had this conversation with you three months ago and you said to me, you know, is there a chronic form of this disease? I would say no. But there have been several papers now that have emerged that describe long haul covid. It's a chronic, debilitating form of this disease.”

Link
The idea of Long Haul Covid gained traction when medical professionals realised they werent getting any better.

V/O
2020 was the start of Pheodah Ngoepe’s medical career. A sterling student she had just graduated from Wits and was about to start her two year internship at hospitals in Port Elizabeth.

She had barely started working when she was seconded to work in the COVID Wards . Like many state hospitals, Livingstone was struggling to cope with the huge influx of people needing desperate medical attention.

Phoeda
“I have unfortunately seen people die from from covid, especially in the time when the hospitals were full.

This is someone who qualifies to be in ICU, but they just don't have the beds. And unfortunately, you just watch them get worse in front of your eyes and there's nothing you can do.”

V/O
Even though she was hyper vigilant about infection control Ngoepe contracted COVID. She had a mild dose, she lost her sense of smell and had a slight cough. After isolating for two weeks she went back to work on the wards.

Pheidah
“The week after that, that's when everything just started to change, I started getting all of the other symptoms of covid, I started getting shortness of breath and struggling with chest pain, getting an unbelievable level of fatigue.”

V/O
One of the most common symptoms is the extreme exhaustion. Ngoepe says that some days even getting up to shower is a mammoth task.

Pheidah
“Now I can’t do much, I can't even go to the grocery store to buy my own groceries because I physically can't carry it. It's just too much for me.”

V/O
It is estimated that about 10 % of COVID patients get Long Haul - Dr Helen van der Plas, an infectious diseases physician in Cape Town, has treated many people living with Long Haul.

Helen
“Earlier reports from Rome you know Italy had a huge outbreak, they were following hopsitalised patients up and saw that after 60 days that more 2/3rds of patients have symptoms and this is unusual to see this in acute viral illness. Of course this is a new disease and everyone is focussed on managing acute illness and getting people to survive.”

V/O
Prof Karim says that science doesn’t fully understand why some people get Long Haul and others don’t.

Karim
“It’s not the virus.The virus is gone. It's the body's reaction to that virus. And in some patients, the body overreacts. It leads to something we call a cytokine storm, where a whole range of signals that trigger many parts of our immune response. It's a bit like your body sending a signal that says send in the Army, send in the Navy, send in the Air Force. We need everybody all hands on deck.”

V/O
2020 was also meant to be Helen Moffat’s dream year her debut novel was sold to international publishers, she was set for book tours and literary festivals and as she says “COVID ate the lot.”

Masa
“How did you cope? I mean, you have to self isolate and you live alone, which is frightening?”

Helen
“It was terrifying. But the merciful thing is, is that by then I was so sick that I don't remember very much.”

V/O
In her delirium she managed to contact her doctor who prescribed steroids for her.

Helen
“Which is interesting because my GP wasn't treating me for covid at that point. In fact, he said to me, according to the World Health Organization, if you had covid by now, you'd either be dead or recovered. So he was just treating me for standard viral pneumonia.

And in doing so, he saved my life.”

V/O
Many patients feel frsutrated as there is no treatement protocol yet.
Ngoepe’s doctors were flumoxed as all her tests came back normal.

Pheidah
“The only tests that I did that came back on abnormal was my C.T. scan, which just showed that my lungs were still recovering from covid. And this was in October. So four months after I had COVID.

Masa
“And how do you treat this?”

Helen
“I think the first thingis to recognise it, acknowledge it, the one thing that we should not be doing, the one thing that we should not be saying as a medical fraternity is that it is going to go away.”

Lucille
“But many patients who experience Long Covid Long Haulers, I think the good news is that they will get better with time.”


V/O
Prof Lucille Blumberg of the National Institude for Communicable Diseases says that South Africa will be doing research on Long Haulers.


Lucille
“I think that’s the one thing we do know is that they don’t pose a risk to thers and they are not infectious and do not need to be in isolation.”

Helen
“I get aaah you are going to infect me and I am like no,let me explain, I don’t have an active covid viral infection but what I am I having is an extreme immune response to having had the virus 8 months ago.”

V/O
Moffat says she is improving slowly but due to exhaustion is only able to work every other day. Ngoepe has not been able to work since August.

Pheida
“The Doctors just can’t explain it and just as there is no cure for acute covid yet there is no cure for long covid yet. So I am just resting and hoping I get better.”

Karim
‘People need to get back to work and back to their lives and they carrying this burden of this disease and my heart goes out to them because I can see the pain that it brings.”

Link
What we noticed while making this programme is a general fatigue around wearing masks

V/O
Despite the fact that figures in South Africa are surging, people just
don’t seem to care.

V/O
There has been the hope in the recent release of several effective vaccines, which will prevent deaths and medical complications. But until then, we have to continue observing strict COVID protocols.





Helen
“And then there is the big thing that really gets my goat is when people say Oh this is all nonsense oh this is a hoax Oh I hope I get this and get it oiver with, the sooner we get it the sooner we are on our way to herd immunity, those people really make me see red and see steam come out of my ears, because truly I would not wish this on my worst enemy.”





Promo 1

Imagine that you caught covid 19 and survived but you never recover from these delbilitating symptoms. This is a the chronic form of Covid 19 and the people living with it are called the Long Haulers.

Promo 2

They are called Long Haulers, survivors grappling with COVID 19 symptoms that continue to linger. About 10 percent of carona virus patients face a life with a severly compromised immune system.

Promo 3

COVID 19 vaccines are in the offing and while they may prevent future infections, there are those who still live with the lingering effects of the virus long after it has left their body. This is called Covid Long Haul.
